title: The Restraint of Trade Clause That Decides What You Can Do the Day After You Sell
linkedin:
Most business owners negotiate hard on the multiple and barely glance at the clause that outlasts it.

The restraint of trade clause is standard in almost every Australian SME sale contract, and it is one of the few terms built to survive settlement completely intact. It sets out what you cannot do next, where, and for how long, usually agreed months before anyone stops to ask what life actually looks like after the sale.

The shape of it tends to follow the shape of the business. A professional services practice usually attracts a clause built around clients and referral relationships rather than a physical territory, because the goodwill being sold is largely personal. A trades or hospitality business is more likely to see a tight geographic radius instead, since the goodwill sits closer to location and foot traffic.

Where it catches owners out is later, not on settlement day. Someone gets approached to consult on something unrelated that a broadly worded clause still technically captures. Or a sale includes an earnout, and the restraint period runs longer than the payment schedule suggested, leaving them tied to a business they no longer control day to day.

This is a term worth shaping before a heads of agreement is signed, not after. Reasonable is judged against what genuinely protects the goodwill being sold, not what a buyer's template happens to include by default.

Full piece on the ProfitPulse blog.

Almost every sale contract includes a restraint of trade clause, and it's one of the few terms built to outlast settlement completely. It sets the industry, the geography and the timeframe you're locked out of once the deal is done.

A note for Brisbane, Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria business owners who are even loosely thinking about a future sale.

Most of the attention in a business sale goes to the price and the multiple. Less attention goes to the restraint of trade clause, even though it is one of the few terms in the contract built to survive settlement completely intact. It sets out what you cannot do next, where you cannot do it, and for how long, and it is usually agreed months before anyone stops to properly consider what life looks like after the sale.

The shape of the clause tends to follow the shape of the business. A professional services practice usually attracts a clause built around clients and referral relationships. A trades or hospitality business is more likely to see a tight geographic radius instead. Neither is automatically unreasonable, but the wording matters enormously, and vague drafting can end up restricting far more of an owner's future than the deal ever intended.

The problems rarely surface on settlement day. They tend to surface later, when an unrelated opportunity turns up that a broadly worded clause still technically captures, or when a restraint period runs longer than an earnout payment schedule suggested it would.
